Anthropic published an incident writeup this week. During a red team cybersecurity exercise, Claude Mythos 5 produced working malware, and one package reached 15 real machines before anyone pulled it back.

A red team exercise exists to produce malware under controlled conditions, so that part went as designed. The package escaped because the test environment had been misconfigured, which gave a sandbox everyone believed was sealed a working route to the public internet.

OpenAI disclosed a similar escape in the same week, with GPT-5.6 Sol getting out of its own sandbox during an evaluation. Two labs hit the same failure within days, and in both cases the trouble started at the network boundary.

Capability questions dominate the agent risk reviews I see, and the vendor owns most of those answers. The network boundary is yours, though, and it deserves the first hour of any review, because an agent's blast radius is set by whatever it can reach.

Anthropic disclosed this on its own rather than waiting for someone else to surface it, and self-reports like that are how the rest of the industry learns anything solid.

If you run agents in production, what can your agents reach outbound today? I'd like to hear how teams handle it. Mentions: @Anthropic, @OpenAI.

Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Max this week with open weights. It scored 53.4 on JobBench, while OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol scored 45.4.

The score means more once you know what JobBench measures. Most benchmarks that circulate grade how well a model answers questions. JobBench grades whether a model completes a piece of work from start to finish, which sits much closer to what a buyer weighs when they evaluate an agent. On that measure, a model you can download currently leads the hosted flagship.

An 8-point gap is a real gap, and it still keeps both models in the same league. A single benchmark with a single scoring setup also says nothing about your own tasks or your own failure modes.

The deployment change runs deeper than the leaderboard. Open weights means you can download the model and run it on infrastructure you control, with no per-token bill arriving at the end of the month, which matters if you carry data residency or procurement constraints. The same release includes a 27B variant that a small team can afford to host.

Hosted pricing moved in the same week too, with OpenAI cutting Luna API pricing by 80%, to $0.20 per million input tokens.

If you shelved an agent project this year over cost or capability, the assumptions under that decision have expired. Re-run the evaluation on your own tasks and see where the options stand now.

If you've re-run that comparison recently, what changed for you? Mentions: @OpenAI.

Black Forest Labs put FLUX 3 into early access this week. It's a single foundation model trained across image, video and audio, and it generates 20 second multilingual video with the sound created in the same pass as the picture.

The same lab then shipped FLUX-mimic, built with mimic robotics. It's a video action model for general purpose robot manipulation, reacting in 101 milliseconds.

Predicting the next frame of a video and choosing a robot's next action are nearly the same computation. Both ask a model what happens next, given what it has seen so far. If that holds up, a video model trained on pixels doubles as a general prediction engine, and robotics becomes a natural second market for a media lab.

On quality, the numbers come from the lab's own preliminary evaluation of an early FLUX 3 candidate, so read them as a vendor grading its own homework. Voters preferred FLUX 3 to Kling v3 Pro in 60% of comparisons. The margin widened to 77% against Runway Gen-4.5 and to 93% against Luma Ray 3.2, while Gemini Omni Flash and Seedance 2.0 held it close at 52%.

Early access is a demo pass, and a 20 second clip is still a clip. The production change available right now is that one model covers picture and sound for short form, which deletes the separate voice pass from that pipeline. If the robotics claim survives outside the lab, the bigger business ends up there.

Do you read FLUX 3 and FLUX-mimic as one bet or two separate products? I'd like to hear the case for two.

77 companies, including Google, Meta, OpenAI and Nvidia, signed an open letter this week asking Washington to keep open, downloadable models unrestricted. Moonshot AI then released Kimi K3 on Hugging Face, a 2.8 trillion parameter model with a 1M token context window, free to download. Within days, US officials alleged Moonshot had built it using Anthropic's Fable without authorization, and sanctions came up. AI experts publicly disputed that account and pointed to real advances in reinforcement learning as the reason the model performs. Officials then stepped back from restricting Chinese open models and moved toward audits and benchmarks.

Precision matters on the Fable claim. It stands as an allegation that experts contested, and repeating it as an established finding would get ahead of the evidence.

The two halves of that story traveled unevenly. The allegation filled the news cycle the day it landed, while the correction that followed moved far more quietly and still ended up steering the policy.

If you run open weights in production, the planning signal sits in that last move. Policy is drifting toward testing models rather than blocking them, which is a different world to plan for than a sanctions regime, and the drift happened inside a week.

Before treating any of this as settled I'd want two answers. Who runs the audits, and against which benchmarks?

If you build on open weights, how do you track policy that moves this fast?

OpenAI launched Presence this week, an enterprise agent platform for support across chat and voice. BBVA, SoftBank and IAG are early customers, and they report that 75% of support issues resolve without a human stepping in.

Treat the 75% carefully. The companies measured it themselves, under their own definition of resolved, so it's a customer claim awaiting outside verification. It still deserves attention, because support economics turn on how many tickets close before they reach a person, and that's exactly what this number claims to move.

Cursor shipped Router in the same week. It sends each coding request to a model matched to the job, and Cursor reports AI coding costs fell 30% to 50% while code quality held or improved.

Both results came from plumbing. Presence gets its number from workflow design, and Router's savings come from a routing decision. Neither waited for a smarter model. That should encourage smaller teams, because both levers work at any size. Route the cheap requests to cheap models, and report the share of volume that closes without a person, since that says more about your support economics than how impressive any single answer sounds.

A caveat belongs in any business case built on the 75%. The remaining quarter holds the angry customers and the ambiguous problems. That work still lands on your team, and it stays the expensive part to staff, so plan headcount around that share.

If you run a support or engineering function, what share of your volume closes without a human today? Real numbers welcome, including the unflattering ones. Mentions: @OpenAI.

SK Hynix reported record profits this week, and within 48 hours South Korea's stock market had halted trading twice while about $590 billion in market value drained away.

The results came in strong. The selloff happened because analysts had priced in something better than a record, so a record was enough to knock the price down. Markets reprice expectations like that all the time, and on a chart the move looks identical to a business stumbling, even though the two say very different things to anyone deciding what to build.

Using AI got cheaper again in the same window, with OpenAI cutting its API pricing by 80%. The infrastructure serving those calls keeps getting more expensive to build, so the AI trade now hangs on whether the buildout pays back on the timeline investors assumed.

The signal to watch from here is capital spending guidance. If companies revise their buildout plans down, the thesis changed. So far the market has only adjusted its own forecast.

If you're planning around AI capacity, which carries more weight for you, the market reaction or the next round of spending guidance? Mentions: @OpenAI.
